text: The real worry isn't that Cassini is a dirty machine, but that it might carry Earth bacteria or other contaminants into a place where life could exist. Saturn's moons, like Enceladus, have hints of conditions that might support life, so scientists want the probe removed from the system rather than drifting around forever, where it could bump into or orbit close to a potentially inhabited moon. The final plunge into Saturn's atmosphere destroys the spacecraft, and any debris burns up. It's a clean way to make sure the probe doesn't linger where it could contaminate the place that might need protecting.

Your stationary leg is doing more work than it looks. When you push off, that leg braces against the ground and takes a sharp load, while the board carries you, so the muscles and joints have to absorb the impact of every stride. If you're still finding a way to keep that leg on the board instead of pushing off, the strain shifts into the quadriceps, hip and ankle in a slightly different pattern, and that's usually what aches afterward.

People often assume the pushing leg does all the work, but the planted leg is the one actually driving you forward and feeling every change in surface. Rough pavement, curbs or even a small lip in the sidewalk can make that bracing leg absorb a lot more than on smooth asphalt. The ankle especially takes it, and if you're landing from a slight drop or rolling over cracks, the joint and the tendons around it get a rougher workout than you'd expect.

One fix that helps is to consciously keep the pushing leg from dragging or scraping the ground, and to shorten your push stride if the ache is in the ankle or knee. That way the planted leg doesn't get overleveraged. If the pain is in the hip, check that you're not twisting while the leg is planted. A tiny bit of torsion on every push can irritate the hip flexors over time.

Warming up before you roll and doing a few minutes of ankle circles, lunges and hip openers takes a lot of the edge off, because the muscles and tendons are less likely to complain when they're cold. And don't ignore it if it keeps coming back, because persistent pain after riding can mean you're pushing too hard for the strength you actually have. It's usually a technique thing, not a gear problem.

Most Americans of African descent aren't actually from Africa, so why are they called Afro-American? It's a bit of a linguistic holdover. The term "Afro-American" is often used to describe people of African descent, but in reality, the majority are not from the continent itself. Instead, the label reflects the cultural connection to Africa. You'll hear it used in contexts like music, fashion, and even academic discussions about identity. It's a way of acknowledging that heritage, even if the person has never set foot on the African continent. So while it might seem contradictory, the term is about cultural roots, not geography.

They get them from the usual places: smuggling runs across the Turkish and Lebanese borders, captures from defeated units, and a handful of local markets where everything is for sale. The reason acquisition never stops is that they're using them up faster than they can replace them. Every skirmish eats through bullets and shells, and whenever a faction loses territory they pick up the loser's guns. Stopping would mean admitting you're losing ground, and nobody in that fight wants to be the one saying that out loud.

That's the whole problem, and it's not a bug. The same systems that give you that rush are the ones that start to misfire. You're asking for the reward without the cost, but the cost isn't a side effect bolted on; it's the price of hijacking the same pathways. Take heroin. You get the euphoria, but your brain stops producing its own dopamine, so once it wears off the floor feels like a cliff. With cocaine it's the reverse: the flood of dopamine gets cut off hard, which is why the crash hits. No drug is a perfect gift that only gives and never takes.

The body notices the imbalance quickly. Tolerance means you need more for the same effect, and then more again. That's not your imagination, it's the system recalibrating. The dependence part is the body treating the drug like it's part of its normal chemistry. When you stop, it's not just "missing the high"; your own production is suppressed, so normal life feels underwhelming. That's why a "zero adverse effects" version basically can't exist.

None of this means all drugs are automatically terrible, just that the pleasure is tied to the cost. Some effects show up later, some right away, and the timing changes how dangerous they feel. A substance that gave pure euphoria with no downsides would have to leave the reward and the withdrawal completely separate, and I don't see how the brain would let that happen.

That's why it feels different from a normal headache. Your legs and lower back are taking the hit from the sustained effort, and the stress and poor posture compound it. Hi,

A few useful things about buying a house that people often miss.

Start with what you can actually borrow before you start touring houses. The bank's decision sets a ceiling, and most people bid far above it. Get the preapproval number first.

Then check what the area actually does in bad weather. Flood zones matter more than the seller admits, and old plumbing is a common surprise. Ask the seller for water bills, not just a thumbs up on the kitchen.

Don't skip the inspection because the house "looks fine." You're buying the building, not the photo.

The mortgage paperwork is the part people underplan for. Your solicitor or lender needs time to chase documents and clear searches. Give them at least three to four weeks before completion.

The biggest risk is falling in love with the house instead of the numbers. Set your budget first, then hunt inside it.

Thanks,
Sam

Great question. They use GPS stations that are bolted directly onto the bedrock. Those stations are super accurate, tracking positions to the centimeter, and comparing readings over years gives you the velocity of the plate itself.

There's also a bunch of other data: ocean floor magnetic stripes, seafloor spreading rates, and fossil distributions all cross-check the numbers. I think the Pacific-North American plate, for example, is moving at a rate you could see on a map in about a human lifetime, but the day-to-day shift is tiny.

It’s not a single measurement. It’s decades of consistent data from many points, all pointing the same direction.

Inbreeding brings together gene copies that are already similar, so harmful recessive variants have a much higher chance of meeting their matching partner. Most of us carry a few of these quietly, but relatives share ancestors, so the odds of both parents carrying the same variant climb quickly.

When that happens, the variant stops hiding in a single copy and gets expressed. A child may inherit two copies of a harmful variant instead of one, which is why rare genetic problems show up more often in related families. It is not some mysterious “blood purity” idea; it is ordinary genetics with changed probabilities.

For IQ, the effect is indirect: the same recessive variants that cause disease or developmental issues can also nudge cognitive development downward. A child can be healthy overall and still carry a small cognitive cost, which is why average IQ trends down a little in closely related lineages. It isn’t a hard rule for every family, and the exact amount of decline varies by which genes are involved.

Pain isn't the same everywhere on the body. The arm is a fairly ordinary, non‑vital spot, with thinner muscle and more fat under the skin, so a hit, shot, or shallow cut there often registers as less intense than the same injury to the torso, ribs, or a joint. That doesn't mean arm injuries are mild; a deep wound or a broken bone still hurts a lot. The difference is mostly about where the injury lands and how much tissue gets involved. Nerve density and how central the area is to movement or breathing also matter. So when someone says an arm injury seems less painful, they're usually talking about the comparison with more sensitive or critical regions, not claiming the arm is pain‑free.

Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it grabs onto hemoglobin in your red blood cells about two hundred times more tightly than oxygen does. Your blood has a job: pick up oxygen in the lungs and carry it around the body. Carbon monoxide sneaks in, parks itself on the hemoglobin, and doesn't let go. Oxygen has to queue behind it. The more CO in your blood, the fewer spots are left for oxygen, so your cells start starving even though your lungs are breathing in perfectly good air.

Carbon dioxide doesn't have that problem. It does bind to hemoglobin, but far more weakly, and it's also a normal waste product your body constantly produces and exhales. Your lungs clear it out with every breath. That's why CO2 only becomes a worry at very high concentrations, like in a sealed room with a crowd or in industrial settings. It's not harmless forever, but it doesn't hijack your oxygen transport the way CO does.

This is why CO is so dangerous in enclosed spaces: heaters, cars, or generators can pump out the gas, and before you notice anything wrong, your blood is already carrying too much CO. The body doesn't have a good way to detect it, which is why people get confused about how you can smell smoke if you can't smell the poison itself. The symptoms are sneaky. Fatigue, headache, dizziness, nausea. It can look like the flu, which is part of the danger.

The treatment is straightforward: move the person into fresh air and give them pure oxygen. In serious cases, a hyperbaric chamber helps displace the CO from hemoglobin faster than ordinary oxygen can. But prevention is much easier: keep vents clear, check heaters, and never run engines in a closed space. The gas is invisible and odorless, so your senses won't save you. Knowing the difference between the two gases is the whole point. Oxygen and CO2 are everyday molecules you're used to, but CO is the intruder that quietly takes the seat.

In an aircraft emergency, the brace position is a way of reducing the forces your body has to take during a hard landing or crash. If you're seated correctly, you lean forward, tuck your chin, and press against the seat in front of you. That keeps your head and chest from snapping forward when the plane stops suddenly.

The position mainly protects the heart, lungs, and brain. By bending your knees and pressing your hands against the seat, you shorten the distance those organs travel, so they take less shock. You also keep your arms away from the headrest and the window side to reduce the chance of your hands injuring your face.

The goal isn't to keep every body part safe, but to give the vital organs a better chance in a serious impact.

There actually were businesses before the industrial era, but they usually didn’t survive because they didn’t scale the way modern companies can. Preindustrial firms were limited in size, depended on local demand and craft knowledge, and often changed hands or folded. Industrial-era firms, with things like standardized processes, mass production and modern management, could grow much bigger. So most of the well-known names we list today were founded in the industrial period or later, which is why the question feels confusing at first.

I walked into a dealership last month wanting to finance a used sedan, and the salesperson kept pointing at the low advertised rate, which felt like the whole deal was a no-brainer. It wasn't. The bank offered a rate only a little higher than the dealer's number, yet my monthly payment came out nearly a hundred dollars lower. That's because the bank is pricing the loan on what I'm actually paying and how my credit looks right now, while the dealer's low rate often sits next to a higher purchase price loaded with fees and extras.

The dealership's low rate can be a hook. The car price gets padded, documentation fees get added, and the monthly number they quote can hide the total you'll actually pay. The bank doesn't have to win you with the sticker, it just runs the numbers on the real transaction. If I take the car from the dealer and finance through the bank, I control the terms instead of letting the dealer stack services on top of a "cheap" rate.

There's also a timing angle. Dealer financing is arranged on the spot, and the rate you're shown often assumes the payment schedule they want you to commit to. A bank can structure the loan around my own cash-flow reality: a longer term if I need it, or a shorter term if I can afford higher payments. That flexibility tends to cost less in the end, even when the headline rate is slightly higher.

I'm not saying banks are automatically better. Some dealers negotiate better rates for loyalty or volume, and a bank's higher rate isn't a deal breaker if the total payment is lower. What matters is the total cost, not the number on the sign. I'd rather see the real purchase price, the real fees, and the real monthly payment before I sign anything. The bank's slightly higher rate is cheaper in practice because I'm not paying for the dealer's extras and I'm not locked into a payment schedule that looks good only until it doesn't.

In the end, the "cheaper" answer isn't about the interest rate at all. It's about the total cost of the transaction. If a dealer's low rate comes with a padded price and hidden fees, the bank's higher rate can still win on the bottom line. The concrete detail that sold me was simple: same car, same dealer, different financing source, and my monthly payment dropped enough that the bank option clearly cost less over the life of the loan.

I still think marijuana should be legal, and not because everyone loves the smell. It's because the states that have legalized it have shown the money goes to the people, not just the coffers of some corporation. Oregon and California are the clearest examples. In Oregon, the tax revenue funds schools, roads and even housing. That's the point. When a state makes cannabis legal, it shouldn't just hand the whole thing to a few big players. The problem is that legalization can quietly become a new monopoly, especially if only big companies can afford the license fees. I'm not saying it's easy to keep small growers in the game, but it has to be a possibility. The best version is one where the little guys can sell a jar of local flower at a farmers market while the state collects its taxes. That feels right to me.

People ask if the body is some kind of bio battery, and that's not quite it. The electricity comes from tiny pumps moving salt ions across cell membranes, and that movement is what actually generates the voltage.

A heart cell can pump potassium in and sodium out, and the resulting charge difference is enough to trigger the whole heartbeat. No sparks, no wires, just chemistry doing its quiet work.

It's not something you can see or feel directly. It's the invisible machinery behind every heartbeat and twitch, and knowing it works this way takes some of the mystery out of "electric" in a human body.

I used to think sampling was just grabbing a hook and letting an auto-tune do the rest, and I was wrong. The interesting part is deciding what you keep and what you throw away, which is where most people get the whole thing backwards.

Start with the source itself. If you can get the original master, you're not stuck with a CD rip or a YouTube stream. The difference in a clean cut of a horn stab or a bass line is night and day, and it makes the sample feel less like an echo of the old record and more like a piece of it.

The chopping is where the music happens. Take a phrase you like and slice it into smaller pieces, sometimes one hit at a time. That's how a single second of a piano phrase turns into a loop you can rearrange. You're not transcribing, you're curating, and the rhythm you build out of those little hits is your contribution, not the original artist's.

Timing is a judgement call I've seen ruin a lot of tracks. If the source is 92 BPM and your song is 120, you have to choose between stretching the sample (which can sound thin and watery) or keeping the source's speed and changing the song. Neither is objectively right. I've landed somewhere in between more than once, and the track ended up feeling more like me than the original, which is the point.

Processing matters less than people claim. A simple low-pass filter and a touch of reverb is often enough to make a 1970s vocal blend into a modern beat. Slap on too much compression or saturation and you've burned the detail out of it.

The legal side keeps getting rediscussed every few years, the same way the five second rule does, and most of that debate is noise. If you're releasing commercially you'll want a license, or you're gambling on the label not caring. For a personal track you don't publish, nobody's auditing your folder of stolen riffs. I'm not a lawyer and I won't argue the rules, but the practical reality is that a good sample has to stand up to the track you're making, not the other way around.

What I've come to believe is that sampling isn't a shortcut. It's an argument about what deserves to survive in your song. The old song gives you the bones, you provide the new shape, and if you're lucky the two actually talk to each other instead of one drowning the other. That's the part I keep finding over and over: you can't automate the decision of whether a fragment belongs in the final mix.

My head hurting isn't the brain itself, which feels counterintuitive. The pain is happening in the membranes wrapping the brain and the blood vessels, which get sensitized and start firing at the slightest touch or change in pressure.

I can picture it: pressing on your forehead or temple makes it worse, not because of some deep brain process, but because the outer layers are what actually send the signal. The "deep ache" people describe tracks with that.

What helps or hurts depends on the trigger. Dehydration, low food, poor sleep, or screen glare will each push it toward a headache, but the sensation of pain lives on the surface. That distinction is worth remembering the next time the throbbing starts.

Can't say if the food is good since we never ate. We got there at 7:20 on Sunday, picked the place because of our 10 p.m. show in the same hotel and assumed it'd be convenient. We joined the digital waitlist, which turned out completely useless, then went back to pay at 8:23. After that we just stood around until 8:40, when staff casually said we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15! We're only a party of two, and they offered zero fixes. If payment and the actual wait are that far apart, tell people upfront so the night isn't a complete waste. Total disaster. Zero stars if that were possible.

I went to the buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. and there was no line at all, which surprised me. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay there.

I was disappointed that steak wasn't offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any.

I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider.

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" comes out as "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pried off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life—well, the under-21 version of it—so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too—the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a “rip-off” way exactly, just... if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing—more must be better—so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal—$99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years back we phoned Rockmount Ranch Wear to order two shirts for my dad. The sales rep wrote down the wrong address, reading our “7” as a “1”, so the order that was meant for 5407 got sent to 5401. The people living there took it to the local UPS store to get it sent back, and then the package just vanished. We didn’t find out until weeks later, and by then we’d already ordered two more shirts.

Rockmount wouldn’t refund the first two. The owner was handling the dispute by then. He admitted the shipment had gone to the wrong address, but said there’d be no refund unless the shirts came back. He even blamed us for not being friendly enough to the residents of 5401, which was just four doors away. We ended up disputing the original charge with our card company, and that’s how we eventually got the credit.
